transcript.text: On November 23rd, 2002, a couple in Palm City, Florida, dropped off their beloved dogs Meko and Marlin at Positively Paradise, a local boarding facility while they traveled to see family for Thanksgiving. Both dogs were happy, healthy, and ready for a short stay. But when the couple returned just 48 hours later, they were greeted with tragedy. Miko was found unresponsive, with yellow fluid around his mouth, while Marlin appeared dehydrated and distressed. rushed to emergency care, MAKO was pronounced dead within minutes. The vet suspected he had been unresponsive for nearly an hour. Marlon was treated for severe dehydration and a painful bacterial infection on his paws. Over the course of Maco and Marlin's stay, 35-year-old Nikki Camerlango, the owner of Positively Paradise, exchanged messages with the couple, assuring them that both dogs were doing well. In one message, Nikki claimed Miko was having a little hard time adjusting, though they've done well, yet the reality was far darker. The couple confronted Nikki about the death, and after several unanswered calls later, Nicky sent only one text saying, I can assure you we took the best possible care of him. Following Mako's death, Martin County Sheriff's deputies and animal control officers attempted a welfare check at Positively Paradise. They were blocked by a lock gate and received no response from Nikki. They made several attempts to reach Nicky by phone at her home, which was connected to the facility, but received no response. Hi, here we'd leave, Nikki, the dog trainer. We would absolutely love to help you. The mailbox is full and cannot accept any messages at this time. Goodbye. Soon after, a detective with the sheriff's office began an investigation into the facility. The results of Mako's necropsy were inconclusive, leaving no grounds for criminal charges. However, animal control discovered other violations. Eight animals were kept in cages without water, leading to civil citations for Positively Paradise. Mako's owners were determined to give his death purpose, vowing to prevent similar tragedies. They expressed, I want to make sure whatever my husband and I can do to help change some of those laws and to help ensure that people like Nikki, who aren't licensed and who aren't providing truly holistic and appropriate care, are not allowed to be in business anymore. The sheriff's office later discovered that, about a year earlier, another individual had boarded his dog at the facility, for a few days. He reported that Nikki lost his dog while running it alongside a golf car, but failed to inform him until a full day later. The dog was missing for eight days, and he was never told beforehand that the facility's exercise routine included running dogs around the block tied to a golf car. Despite these incidents, Nikki continued to operate her business for another year, until a second report surfaced of a dog dying under her care. In March 2004, another devastating incident occurred. A woman boarded her healthy golden doodle Flurry at Positively Paradise. Days later, she received a call from Nikki, saying Flurry was unresponsive. It was only after the incident that the owner learned of Mako's case. Although Nikki claimed Furry's condition was pre-existing, Flurry's vet confirmed that the dog was healthy prior to boarding. The sheriff's office reported that Nikki's company license was active in 2023, but was not renewed in 2025. They noted that although no criminal charges had been filed, there were significant concerns. When a news station contacted Nikki, she commented, I understand they lost their pet, and I get it, that's horrible. I wouldn't wish that on anyone, but as a business owner, I don't feel like I need to be taken down. Nikki claimed she had not mistreated any animals and insisted both dogs at pre-existing conditions before arriving, saying Mako suffered from pneumonia and Flurry had an oxygen issue. However, MAKO's necropsy showed no signs of viral or bacterial pneumonia, and although Flurry had kennel cough several months earlier, her veterinarian considered her healthy. Nikki told reporters that she planned to continue her work, saying, this is what I do. I'm a master dog trainer. I nationally certified. The sheriff's office, aware that two otherwise healthy dogs had died under her care, expressed that she should not be involved in animal care. Nonetheless, Nikki still faced no criminal charges, and the sheriff's office. the investigation into Positively Paradise remained open. Days after the story circulated in the news, a third person came forward, recounting the loss of her pet at the facility. She explained that in 2018, she had left her four-month-old Rottweiler, Red, at Positively Paradise for a week of training. Then she received a call from Nikki, asking her to come in because Red's back legs were no longer working and he couldn't stand. Nikki claimed Redd had contracted Parvo, a deadly virus, possibly from a rabbit or squirrel. Since Red hadn't yet received his final parvo booster, the owner initially accepted this explanation. However, her veterinarian later raised concerns, but offered a completely different diagnosis. Red at a bruised trachea, and his spinal cord appeared severed. The virus wasn't to blame. The only option left was to put Red down. When approached by news reporters for comment, Nikki stated, they painted it to seem like I run a torture camp, which isn't accurate at all. These dogs are my life, she added that she intended to continue training dogs elsewhere. Later that month, the sheriff's office was notified of yet another dog death at Positively Paradise, marking the fourth fatality under Nikki's care. According to the owners, Nikki had picked up their two dogs from their residence, but just a few hours later, they received a call from her stating that Bo, their two-year-old male Kavapu, was found unresponsive in a kennel where she had placed him after grooming. The owner soon learned of other news stories detailing similar. incidents involving Nikki's care and reported Bo's death to the Sheriff's Office. They arranged for a forensic analyst specializing in necropcies and animal cruelty cases to examine Bo. Despite repeated attempts, the Sheriff's Office was unable to reach Nikki. They eventually spoke with her father, who shared that Nikki had been receiving death threats due to the dog fatalities. He added that she had been training dogs since age 12, has a deep love for animals, and has never encountered issues before. In June 24, the the sheriff's office received the final report from the forensic analyst who investigated Bo's death. The analyst confirmed that the histopathology indicated blunt-forged trauma to the head, revealing an intracranial hemorrhage. According to the doctor, a significant impact to the head is necessary to cause such an injury. Additionally, Bo suffered blunt-forged trauma to the stomach, chest, and eye. Following the sheriff's office investigation, the necropsy findings and statements made by Nikki, there was probable cause to believe that Nikki intentionally inflicted blunt-forced trauma to Beau's head, leading to his tragic death. As a result, a warrant for Nikki's arrest was issued. On June 19th, Martin County Sheriff's Detectives, with support from the St. Lucy County Sheriff's Office, located Nikki in Fort Pierce, where she had reportedly relocated her dog training and boarding business after Martin County launched a criminal investigation into the death. Meanwhile, Nikki's court proceedings are still ongoing. Since the media coverage of the investigation into Nikki's practices, a wave of troubling accounts emerged.
